The History of Distributed Computing

Distributed computing has evolved dramatically over the past several decades,
transforming from a niche academic pursuit into the backbone of modern technology
infrastructure. This document traces the key developments, ideas, and systems
that shaped the field.

The roots of distributed computing can be traced to the 1960s and 1970s, when
researchers first began connecting computers over networks. The ARPANET, funded
by the United States Department of Defense, became operational in 1969 and
connected four university nodes. This early network demonstrated that geographically
separated computers could communicate and share resources effectively.

In the 1970s, Xerox PARC developed the Ethernet protocol, which enabled local
area networks. Bob Metcalfe's original Ethernet specification operated at 2.94
megabits per second. This technology made it practical for organizations to
connect dozens or hundreds of computers within a single building or campus.

The concept of remote procedure calls (RPC) emerged in the early 1980s through
the work of Bruce Jay Nelson at Xerox PARC and Andrew Birrell at DEC. RPC
allowed programs on one machine to invoke procedures on another machine as if
they were local function calls. This abstraction became foundational for
distributed system design. Sun Microsystems later popularized RPC with their
Open Network Computing implementation.

Concurrent with RPC development, Leslie Lamport published his seminal 1978 paper
on logical clocks, introducing the "happens-before" relationship that provided
a way to reason about ordering of events in distributed systems. His later work
on the Paxos consensus algorithm (first submitted in 1989, published in 1998)
solved the problem of achieving agreement among distributed processes in the
presence of failures.
Page 2

The 1990s brought the World Wide Web and the explosive growth of the internet.
Tim Berners-Lee's invention at CERN in 1989-1991 created a simple yet powerful
distributed system: web browsers communicated with web servers using HTTP, and
documents were linked through URLs. The web demonstrated that distributed systems
could be made accessible to ordinary users, not just computer scientists.

The challenge of building reliable distributed systems was formalized by Eric
Brewer in 2000 with the CAP theorem, later proved by Seth Gilbert and Nancy
Lynch. The theorem states that a distributed system cannot simultaneously provide
all three of the following guarantees: Consistency (every read receives the most
recent write), Availability (every request receives a response), and Partition
tolerance (the system continues to operate despite network partitions). This
insight forced system designers to make explicit tradeoffs.

Google published three papers that transformed large-scale distributed computing.
The Google File System paper (2003) described a scalable distributed file system
for large data-intensive applications. The MapReduce paper (2004) introduced a
programming model for processing large datasets across clusters of computers.
The Bigtable paper (2006) described a distributed storage system for structured
data. These papers inspired the creation of Apache Hadoop and the broader big
data ecosystem.

Amazon contributed equally transformative ideas. Werner Vogels and the Amazon
team published the Dynamo paper in 2007, describing a highly available key-value
store that used techniques like consistent hashing, vector clocks, and sloppy
quorums. Dynamo inspired Apache Cassandra, Riak, and other distributed databases.
Amazon Web Services, launched in 2006, made distributed computing infrastructure
available on-demand through cloud services.
Page 3

The 2010s saw the emergence of container orchestration as a dominant paradigm for
distributed systems. Docker, released in 2013, popularized operating-system-level
virtualization through containers. Google open-sourced Kubernetes in 2014, drawing
on their internal experience with Borg and Omega cluster management systems.
Kubernetes provided a declarative approach to managing containerized applications
across clusters of machines.

The microservices architectural style, popularized by Martin Fowler and James
Lewis around 2014, advocated decomposing applications into small, independently
deployable services. Each service would own its data, communicate via APIs, and
be developed by a small team. This approach enabled organizations like Netflix,
Uber, and Spotify to scale their engineering organizations alongside their systems.

Stream processing systems emerged to handle real-time data. Apache Kafka, originally
developed at LinkedIn and open-sourced in 2011, provided a distributed event
streaming platform. Apache Flink and Apache Spark Streaming offered frameworks
for processing unbounded streams of data. These systems enabled use cases like
real-time analytics, event-driven architectures, and complex event processing.

The concept of serverless computing, pioneered by AWS Lambda in 2014, abstracted
away server management entirely. Developers could write functions that were
triggered by events, with the cloud provider handling all infrastructure concerns.
This represented a further evolution in the level of abstraction available to
developers building distributed applications.

Consensus algorithms continued to evolve. Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout
published the Raft consensus algorithm in 2014, designed to be more understandable
than Paxos while providing equivalent guarantees. Raft was adopted by etcd (the
key-value store underlying Kubernetes), CockroachDB, and other distributed systems.
Page 4

Looking forward, several trends are shaping the future of distributed computing.

Edge computing pushes computation closer to data sources, reducing latency for
applications like autonomous vehicles, augmented reality, and industrial IoT.
Rather than sending all data to centralized cloud data centers, edge computing
processes data at the network edge, with only aggregated results transmitted
to the cloud.

WebAssembly (Wasm) is emerging as a portable runtime for distributed workloads.
Originally designed for web browsers, Wasm provides a sandboxed execution
environment that can run at near-native speed across different architectures.
Projects like Fermyon Spin and Cosmonic are building distributed application
platforms on top of Wasm.

Quantum computing, while still in its early stages, promises to solve certain
classes of problems exponentially faster than classical computers. Distributed
quantum computing systems may eventually enable new forms of parallel processing
and secure communication through quantum key distribution.

The ongoing challenge of building correct distributed systems has led to increased
interest in formal verification. Tools like TLA+ (created by Leslie Lamport)
and Alloy allow engineers to specify and check the properties of distributed
protocols before implementation. Amazon has reported using TLA+ extensively to
verify the correctness of critical distributed systems at AWS.

As distributed computing continues to evolve, the fundamental challenges identified
decades ago -- consensus, fault tolerance, consistency, and partition tolerance --
remain central. What has changed is the scale, the tooling, and the level of
abstraction available to engineers building the next generation of distributed
systems.
